overview: The Federal Aviation Administration halted flights nationwide for nearly five hours on Friday, the longest such stop since Sept. 11, 2001; more than 8,200 flights were canceled, France 24 reported, and cancellations continued into Saturday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed overloaded, decades-old communications equipment, ruled out foul play and asked Congress for $50 billion to overhaul air traffic control. The White House confirmed that President Trump will meet China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin together next week in Shenzhen, the first three-way meeting of those leaders. Nvidia shares fell again in the aftermath of Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive, the Supreme Court agreed to decide whether Trump may bar most asylum claims at the southern border, and in New Orleans officials said everyone aboard a river cruise ship survived after a tanker struck it on the Mississippi.

stories.headline: Flights resume after FAA's nationwide ground stop, but thousands are still canceled
stories.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration halted all U.S. departures for nearly five hours on Friday after a communications failure in the air traffic control system. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed decades-old equipment and asked for more money to replace it; officials said there was no sign of an attack. Flights resumed Friday night, but airlines were still canceling thousands of flights on Saturday.
stories.why_it_matters: Anyone flying this weekend should expect cancellations and long delays while airlines move planes and crews back into place. The failure also puts the age of the air traffic control system, and who pays to replace it, in front of Congress.
stories.background: A ground stop is an FAA order that keeps planes from taking off; they are usually limited to one airport or region for weather or equipment trouble. A nationwide stop is rare. The air traffic control system relies on telecommunications equipment that the Transportation Department itself describes as decades old, and it has had several regional failures, including an outage in September that halted flights into major East Coast airports. Sean Duffy runs the Transportation Department, which oversees the FAA; Markwayne Mullin runs the Department of Homeland Security.

facts.text: The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday, citing "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety."
The stop lasted nearly five hours and was the longest nationwide ground stop since Sept. 11, 2001.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the cause was a communications outage in aging air traffic control technology, and officials said routers had been overloaded with data.
The administration ruled out foul play, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a threat or attack.
Duffy called for more FAA funding to speed up equipment upgrades.
More than 8,200 flights, over 31% of those scheduled in the United States, were canceled on Friday.
Thousands more flights were canceled on Saturday as airlines repositioned planes and crews; Axios put the early-Saturday figure at 3,000.
JetBlue canceled most of its remaining Friday flights and said it expected disruptions to continue the next day.
Some college football games were delayed because of the travel disruption.

stories.headline: Van Hollen challenges Schumer for Senate majority leader and rules out a 2028 run
stories.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is running against Chuck Schumer to lead Senate Democrats, who won back the majority in last week's midterms. Van Hollen said he would not run for president so he could focus on the contest. Schumer's allies say he has well over the votes he needs, and few senators have publicly backed the challenger so far.
stories.why_it_matters: The majority leader decides what the Senate votes on, so the winner will shape how hard Democrats press on the Iran war, corporate power and the filibuster over the next two years.
stories.background: Chuck Schumer of New York has led Senate Democrats since 2017. Democrats won control of the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms, and the party's senators choose their own leader in an internal vote. Some Democratic voters and officeholders have argued since President Trump returned to office that Schumer has not confronted the administration forcefully enough. Van Hollen, a second-term senator from Maryland, is running as the candidate of that wing of the party; Schumer's supporters say the challenge is really about ending the filibuster, the rule that lets 41 senators block most bills.

stories.headline: Supreme Court will decide whether Trump can block asylum claims at the southern border
stories.summary: The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear the Trump administration's appeal of lower-court rulings that found it illegal to shut off asylum applications at the U.S.-Mexico border. The policy stems from an executive order that called the situation at the border an "invasion." The justices will now decide whether a president can suspend access to the asylum system that way.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling will determine whether people who reach the southern border can ask for protection from persecution, and how far a president can go in setting aside immigration law by proclamation.
stories.background: Federal law lets people who reach the United States apply for asylum if they fear persecution at home. On his first day back in office in January 2025, President Trump signed an order declaring an "invasion" at the southern border and directing officials to remove people who cross illegally without the usual chance to seek asylum. Immigrant-rights groups sued, and lower courts, including the federal appeals court in Washington, ruled against the policy. The administration asked the Supreme Court in August to take the case.

stories.headline: Bessent blames Lutnick's Commerce Department over Nvidia chips reaching China
stories.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly faulted the Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for not blacklisting Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of passing advanced AI chips to China. Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, on Dec. 10 according to CBS News. China warned Washington against new export controls, days before President Trump is due to meet Xi Jinping.
stories.why_it_matters: The dispute is about whether U.S. rules meant to keep advanced AI chips from China are being enforced, and it has put a cabinet secretary's job in question a week before a summit with Beijing.
stories.background: The United States restricts sales of the most advanced AI chips to China, and the Commerce Department enforces those rules, in part by adding companies to a trade blacklist called the Entity List. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigned this week after admitting to an affair, following reports that a woman he was involved with was suspected of spying for China; she once led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and China denies the spying allegation. Lawmakers from both parties have asked what the administration knew and why Megaspeed was not restricted.

Lawmakers have also summoned former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to testify.
China warned the United States against imposing new export controls on semiconductors.

stories.headline: Trump administration gives states six more months on Medicaid work requirements
stories.summary: The Trump administration said on Friday that it would delay enforcement of new Medicaid work requirements by six months. The rules still formally take effect Jan. 1, but states can now wait until July to start enforcing them. State officials had warned they were not ready.
stories.why_it_matters: Millions of low-income adults who would have had to prove they work, volunteer or attend school to keep health coverage from January now have until at least July in states that take the extra time.
stories.background: Medicaid is the government health insurance program for low-income people, run by states with federal money. The tax and spending law Republicans passed last year, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, requires many able-bodied adult enrollees to document work, volunteering or schooling to keep coverage, starting Jan. 1, 2027. States have to build systems to check that paperwork, and state officials and health policy groups said the deadline was too tight. Opponents of the rules say eligible people will lose coverage over paperwork; supporters say the rules encourage work.

stories.headline: Everyone survives after a tanker hits a river cruise ship in New Orleans
stories.summary: A tanker struck a river cruise ship on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans on Friday, leaving the passenger vessel partly submerged. Officials said all passengers and crew were accounted for, with no deaths or critical injuries; 32 people were taken to hospitals. The cause has not been determined.
stories.why_it_matters: The Mississippi at New Orleans is one of the country's busiest shipping lanes and a tourist draw, and the collision raises questions about the safety of large cargo ships passing close to passenger boats.
stories.background: Ocean-going tankers and cargo ships share the Mississippi River at New Orleans with riverboats that carry tourists on cruises. On Friday a tanker hit one of those cruise ships near the port, and the passenger vessel rolled onto its side and partly sank, prompting a large rescue operation. Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry and the city's mayor both called the outcome a "miracle on the Mississippi." Investigators have not said what went wrong.

facts.text: A tanker collided with a river cruise ship on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans on Friday, partially submerging the passenger vessel.
Officials said all passengers and crew were accounted for and that no one was killed or critically hurt.
Thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals.

The tanker is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese shipbuilder, and a maritime law expert said videos point to some kind of catastrophic system failure on the vessel, though it is too early to know the cause.

stories.headline: Late midterm calls: Boebert loses her House seat and a Democrat wins Alaska's governorship
stories.summary: Ten days after the midterms, two more races were called for Democrats. Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert in Colorado's 4th District, and Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the Alaska governor's race, the first Democrat to do so since 1998.
stories.why_it_matters: Both results came in places that usually vote Republican, adding to the Democratic gains that will shape the next Congress and state governments.
stories.background: The Nov. 3 midterm elections gave Democrats control of Congress, and some close races took more than a week to count. Lauren Boebert, a three-term Republican and prominent supporter of President Trump, moved from western Colorado to the more conservative 4th District before the 2024 election. Alaska elects its governor by ranked-choice voting, in which voters rank candidates and lower-ranked choices are counted if no one wins a majority outright. Trump had endorsed Republican Bernadette Wilson to succeed Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican who is leaving office.

facts.text: Democrat Eileen Laubacher defeated Rep. Lauren Boebert in Colorado's 4th Congressional District, according to race calls on Friday.
Laubacher is a retired Navy rear admiral; Boebert is a three-term Republican.
The margin was narrow, and Laubacher had claimed victory on Nov. 9 while votes were still being counted.
Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a 37-year-old former state legislator, won the Alaska governor's race and will be the youngest governor in the state's history.
He is the first Democrat elected governor of Alaska since 1998.
President Trump had endorsed Republican Bernadette Wilson in the race to succeed Gov. Mike Dunleavy.
The New York Post reported that Democrats will hold the governor's office in 30 states.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first three-way meeting in Shenzhen next week
stories.summary: The White House said President Trump will meet China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin together on Thursday, Nov. 19, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen. Trump plans to raise cuts to nuclear arsenals and the war in Iran; US officials said Ukraine is not expected to be a focus, and a senior US official does not expect an agreement.
stories.why_it_matters: The three countries hold most of the world's nuclear weapons, so any move toward limits, or a failure to reach one, affects global security. What is left off the agenda, including Ukraine, is also being watched by US allies.
stories.background: The leaders of the United States, China and Russia have never held a formal three-way meeting. The idea was discussed publicly for months, with the Kremlin saying in September that it could happen at the APEC forum, which China hosts this year in Shenzhen. Trump has said he wants talks on reducing nuclear weapons to include China as well as Russia; the last US-Russia treaty capping strategic warheads, New START, expired in February 2026. China has a much smaller arsenal than the other two and has resisted joining three-way arms talks. The meeting comes while the US is at war with Iran and is mediating talks between Russia and Ukraine.

facts.text: The White House said Trump, Xi and Putin will meet on the sidelines of the APEC forum in Shenzhen on Thursday, Nov. 19.
It would be the first formal trilateral meeting of the leaders of the US, China and Russia.
A White House spokeswoman said Trump will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons; a senior US official said no agreement is expected.
US officials said the talks will also cover the war in Iran and are not expected to focus on Russia's war in Ukraine.
Reuters reported that Trump and Putin pushed for the meeting and that Xi has been wary of hosting it.
China's Foreign Ministry said in October that asking China to join three-way nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage would be unrealistic, Al Jazeera reported on Nov. 6.

stories.headline: Zelensky says US envoys asked if Ukraine would give up Donbas for NATO membership
stories.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said US negotiators asked, for the first time, whether Ukraine would withdraw from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for joining NATO; he repeated that Kyiv will not retreat from its territory. The remark followed US-mediated talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi. Separately, the EU named a team from five countries plus the bloc itself to represent Europe at the next round, while both sides kept up heavy air attacks.
stories.why_it_matters: A trade of territory for NATO membership would redraw Europe's borders and commit the US and its allies to defend Ukraine, with consequences for security and defense spending well beyond the region.
stories.background: Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and claims the Donbas, made up of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, part of which Ukraine still holds. Ukraine has long sought NATO membership, which Russia opposes. The Trump administration, through envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, has been mediating; the two met Putin in Moscow on Thursday and then briefed Zelensky in Dublin. European governments have pressed for a place at the talks, and Ukraine wants them there as a counterweight.

Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least seven people and injured 80, the Kyiv Independent reported citing local authorities; Zaporizhzhia's governor said three were killed there, including a child.
A car bomb in Moscow, the second in Russia in two days, wounded Sergei Zavorotny, a former aide to exiled Ukrainian ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov.

Democratic senators Jeanne Shaheen and Chris Coons told Elon Musk to preserve records on SpaceX's restrictions on Ukraine's Starlink and Starshield service; Zelensky accused SpaceX of not being honest about what he called political reasons for the slowdown.

stories.headline: Iran says it destroyed a US radar in Bahrain; US says it shot the drones down
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik, Iran. The US military confirmed an attack but said it shot down two Iranian drones and denied the radar was hit. Iran also reported tankers striking mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and Reuters reported that Trump has told advisers he may hold off on new attacks unless provoked.
stories.why_it_matters: It is the first reported Iranian attack on a US installation in months, and fighting around the Strait of Hormuz affects the oil and gas shipments that feed into fuel prices worldwide.
stories.background: The US and Israel are at war with Iran, a conflict that outlets describe as having settled into a lower level of fighting in recent months. The US Navy is blockading Iranian ports, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard says the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passage for a large share of the world's oil and gas, is closed. Bahrain hosts a large US naval presence. The UN's International Atomic Energy Agency has had no access to key Iranian nuclear sites since Israel and the US struck them during a 12-day conflict in June 2025.

The Revolutionary Guard said two tankers hit sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran's navy said Saturday that an oil tanker was on fire after hitting a mine, Reuters reported.
The UK's maritime trade monitor, UKMTO, had not reported the gas tanker incident Iran described, NewsNation said.
The Revolutionary Guard says the strait is closed; the US Navy says it has opened a southern route for commercial ships while keeping its blockade of Iranian ports.

The International Atomic Energy Agency urged Iran to take steps toward inspections; CBS News, citing a leaked report, said the agency is 'increasingly concerned' about access to a key uranium facility.
Trump has told advisers he may hold off on attacks on Iran barring new provocations, Reuters reported, citing sources.

stories.headline: Microsoft says services are fully restored after a global outage
stories.summary: Microsoft said Saturday that Outlook, Teams, Copilot and its other affected services have recovered, ending an outage that disrupted businesses, governments and public services in many countries. The company apologized and said it was still watching a backlog of delayed email for business customers. The summaries reviewed here do not state a cause.
stories.why_it_matters: Many workplaces, schools and government offices run on Microsoft's email and meeting tools, so an outage of this length stops ordinary work and can cost small businesses real money.
stories.background: Microsoft 365 is the company's online suite of work software, including Outlook email, Teams chat and video meetings, and the Copilot AI assistant. It is used by companies, schools and governments around the world, which means a failure in Microsoft's systems reaches many countries at once. The outage began earlier in the week and Microsoft restored services in stages, with consumer products recovering before business ones. The Guardian described it as one of the worst IT failures in years.

stories.headline: France deploys 70,000 police for a fifth Saturday of anti-government protests
stories.summary: France expected 50 to 60 marches on Saturday and planned to mobilize about 70,000 police and gendarmes, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said. stories.background: France has seen weeks of anti-government demonstrations that began with student protests and blockades of high schools nearly two months ago. They have broadened to include complaints about living costs and about how police have handled the marches, and some have turned into riots. Yellow Vest protesters, known for the 2018-2019 fuel-tax demonstrations, have joined. The unrest comes ahead of a presidential election next year.

stories.headline: Pope Leo XIV returns to Chiclayo, the Peruvian city where he was bishop
stories.summary: Pope Leo XIV drew very large crowds in Chiclayo, in northern Peru, where he served as bishop for eight years, and said it was a 'joy' to be back. stories.background: Leo XIV, born Robert Prevost in Chicago, was elected pope in May 2025, the first from the United States. He spent many years in Peru as a missionary and was bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, becoming a Peruvian citizen along the way. Residents there still call him Father Robert, the New York Times reported. According to France 24, the tour faced fears of cancellation after he had surgery for lung cancer.

stories.headline: South Sudan postpones its first national elections again, to February 2027
stories.summary: South Sudan has moved its presidential and legislative elections from Dec. 22 to Feb. 11, 2027. It would be the country's first national vote since independence in 2011, and it has been delayed several times before. The United Nations had warned that holding the vote could set off widespread conflict.
stories.why_it_matters: South Sudan's 2018 peace deal depends on elections that keep slipping, and renewed fighting there would deepen one of the world's largest humanitarian crises. No right-leaning outlet in the day's feed covered the story.
stories.background: South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011 and fell into civil war in 2013. A 2018 peace agreement set up a transitional government under President Salva Kiir that was supposed to lead to elections, but the vote has been pushed back repeatedly. In 2024 the government extended the transition to February 2027 and moved elections from December 2024 to December 2026, a step the UN called regrettable.

stories.headline: Taiwan says China is running unannounced drills as 'silent intimidation'
stories.summary: Taiwanese officials said China has staged unannounced military exercises in the Pacific this month, at one point massing more than 100 navy and coast guard vessels in the region. France 24 reported that the drills simulated a blockade of the island but that, contrary to some social media claims, no blockade was put in place. Only center-rated outlets in the day's feed covered the story.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan makes most of the world's advanced computer chips and sits on major shipping lanes, so a real blockade or conflict would disrupt electronics supplies and trade globally. Coverage here comes from center-rated outlets only.
stories.background: China claims self-governed Taiwan as its territory and has not ruled out using force to take it; Taiwan's government rejects the claim. Beijing has stepped up military pressure around the island over the past five years, often with large named exercises announced in advance. Taiwanese officials say the latest activity differs in that it was not announced. The drills come days before Xi Jinping hosts Trump and Putin at the APEC forum in Shenzhen.

stories.headline: Nvidia posts sixth straight weekly loss as chip and AI stocks slide after Huang's exit
stories.summary: Nvidia shares fell again on Friday, closing a sixth straight week of declines, the longest such run since 2012, according to CNBC and MarketWatch. Other chipmakers and AI-linked stocks fell with it, and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq ended the day lower while the Dow was little changed. The board is looking for a permanent successor to Jensen Huang, who resigned Thursday; the Financial Times reported an approach to Arm chief Rene Haas, while the board said it had not formally engaged any candidate.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is one of the largest holdings in the index funds that fill most retirement accounts, so its slide reaches people who never bought the stock, CBS News reported. Its earnings next week will show whether the business itself is holding up.
stories.background: Nvidia makes the processors that run most AI data centers, and its rise made it one of the most valuable companies in the world. Co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive and board member on Nov. 12 after news reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes was a Chinese asset. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim CEO while the board searches for a replacement. The stock had already been falling since early October, CNBC reported, so the resignation added to an existing slide. Investors use the term "AI trade" for the group of chip, cloud and data-center stocks that have risen on spending on artificial intelligence.

facts.text: Nvidia's stock fell for a sixth consecutive week, its longest weekly losing streak since 2012.
Nvidia lost $573 billion in market value this week, MarketWatch reported.
Nvidia's market value has fallen by $1.7 trillion during the slide, which began in early October, before Huang's resignation, CNBC reported.
Shares of so-called neocloud companies and other AI stocks fell again on Friday, Reuters reported.
AMD and other chip stocks fell on Friday; MarketWatch said investors had at first treated Nvidia's trouble as a possible gain for rivals.
U.S. stocks declined on Friday as Nvidia shares fell again, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The New York Times reported that the drop in Nvidia shares had not spread to the rest of the market, and Bloomberg said stocks finished the week higher.
Nvidia said in a Nov. 12 securities filing that Huang resigned effective immediately and that Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO while remaining chief financial officer.
Nvidia's board said it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the CEO role, The Japan Times reported.
Some Nvidia employees are calling for Huang to return, according to The Japan Times and France 24.
Nvidia lacks full insurance coverage for damages stemming from the conduct of executives and is exposed to possible lawsuits, the Financial Times reported.
Before his exit Huang called Kress "a deer in the headlights," and Kress had questioned some of his dealmaking, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The Hindu carried a report that Huang twice described his dealings with Alice Huang and the chip buyer Megaspeed as appropriate when press inquiries drew the attention of Nvidia leaders, and that he misled the company's top lawyer.
The fall in Nvidia shares cut the value of Huang's own stake by more than $20 billion over five days, Fox Business reported.
Millions of Americans hold Nvidia shares indirectly through retirement plans and index funds, CBS News reported.
Financial advisers polled by CNBC said investors should weigh their Nvidia exposure, time horizon and risk tolerance before reacting to the leadership change.
Nvidia is due to report earnings next week, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Goldman Sachs forecast that the S&P 500 will rise to 8,700 next year despite slower earnings growth, Reuters reported.

stories.summary: The International Energy Agency said global oil supply exceeded demand by almost 2 million barrels a day in October, the first surplus since the Iran war began, The Guardian reported. stories.headline: Flatbush collapse: Times reports developer avoided stricter oversight; medical examiner rules on deaths
stories.summary: Three days after a building on Flatbush Avenue collapsed, the New York Times reported that the developer of the project next door first won approval for a three-story building and then sought to add floors, which kept the project out of the stricter oversight that larger projects get. The Daily News reported that the medical examiner found all of the victims suffocated in the rubble. An injured construction worker has hired a lawyer and alleges corners were cut at the site, the New York Post reported. No official cause has been announced.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday that eight people died, including two children, and more than a dozen others were hurt; the dead included residents and construction workers. Rescue crews finished searching the rubble on Thursday, and the Brooklyn district attorney opened a criminal inquiry. The Department of Buildings is the city agency that approves and inspects construction projects.

stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Friday that President Donald Trump agreed, after the two spoke directly, to delay enforcement of new federal rules requiring stores that accept food stamps to stock a wider range of staple foods. stories.headline: Mamdani moves to break up NYPD's Strategic Response Group; outlets differ on whether it is disbanded or renamed
stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani is overhauling the Strategic Response Group, the NYPD unit that responds to protests and also does counterterrorism work. The New York Times reported that the unit's crowd-control and counterterrorism duties will be spread among other units, including a new Civilian Dialogue Unit. City & State reported that the mayor will also back a City Council bill, the CURB Act, aimed at the unit.
stories.why_it_matters: The change affects how police handle demonstrations in the city and who responds to large emergencies. Disbanding the unit was a campaign promise, and New Yorkers on both sides of the policing debate will be watching whether practice on the street changes.
stories.background: The Strategic Response Group is an NYPD unit of about 500 officers that responds to protests, counterterrorism operations and other large events. Civil liberties groups and some council members have criticized its handling of demonstrations, and Mamdani has pledged since his campaign to disband it and to separate protest response from counterterrorism. Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch told the City Council in March that talks were about changing how the city polices protests, 'not to disband' the unit, and the mayor said he was prepared to overrule her. The CURB Act, sponsored by Council Member Chi Ossé, would disband the unit by law and includes a provision meant to stop the department from recreating it under another name; in July it was one co-sponsor short of a Council majority, the Amsterdam News reported.

stories.summary: The city completed the safety redesign of a one-mile stretch of McGuinness Boulevard in Greenpoint on Friday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced alongside other elected officials. The project began after a teacher was killed by a driver on the road in 2021 and stalled for years under the previous mayor.
stories.why_it_matters: McGuinness is a main route through north Brooklyn for drivers, cyclists and people on foot, and the new layout changes how all of them use it. The project is also an early test of the mayor's promise to finish street safety work that stalled under his predecessor.
stories.background: Matthew Jensen, a public school teacher, was struck and killed by a driver on McGuinness Boulevard in 2021, and neighbors campaigned for a redesign. The city planned to cut car traffic to one lane in each direction and add protected bike lanes, but the Adams administration halted the full plan and allowed only a shortened version to go ahead in 2024. The project later figured in the bribery case against Ingrid Lewis-Martin, a former top aide to Mayor Eric Adams, who has pleaded not guilty. Mamdani ordered the full design built in his first week in office, and the Department of Transportation broke ground in May.

facts.text: The redesign of a one-mile stretch of McGuinness Boulevard was completed Friday, and Mamdani and other elected officials marked the occasion.
The redesign followed the death a little over five years ago of Matthew Jensen, a public school teacher who was hit by a driver on the boulevard.
The project went through years of starts and stops and played a part in the bribery case of a former top aide to Mayor Eric Adams, THE CITY reported.
Mamdani directed the city in early January to build the full redesign.
The Department of Transportation broke ground on the full redesign in late May.

markets.summary: Stocks ended Friday mixed, and Nvidia was again the reason. The S&P 500 fell 0.40% and the technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 0.91%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average, which holds fewer AI-related companies, rose 0.10%. Nvidia shares dropped for a sixth straight week, their longest weekly losing streak since 2012 according to CNBC, and MarketWatch reported the company lost $573 billion in market value this week alone after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive; Reuters and MarketWatch said other chip and AI stocks slid with it. Interest rates are the second pressure: the 10-year Treasury yield, the rate the government pays to borrow for a decade, was at 5.10% in the latest reading, and Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee told CNBC the central bank "has definitely got work to do" on inflation. Some rows in the quote table are older than a day: Treasury yields are from Nov. 12, oil from Nov. 11 and currencies from Nov. 6.

movers.name: Nasdaq Composite
movers.why: Fell 0.91% on Friday as Nvidia and other chip and AI stocks slid again; MarketWatch reported investors are rethinking the AI trade after Jensen Huang's departure. The index is down 5.83% over the past month.

movers.name: Dow Jones Industrial Average
movers.why: Rose 0.10% while the other major indexes fell. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's drop has not spread to the rest of the market, and the Dow is up 1.41% over the past month.

movers.name: Bitcoin
movers.why: Bitcoin fell 3.73% to about $68,200 and is down 16.54% in a month. Fox Business tied the slide to the Nvidia selloff, and MarketWatch reported that some investors may sell crypto to buy into Anthropic's upcoming stock offering; the exact cause is not settled.

movers.name: 10-year Treasury yield
movers.why: The 10-year Treasury yield rose 12 basis points (0.12 percentage point) to 5.10% on Nov. 12, the latest figure in the table, as investors weighed higher inflation and the chance of further Federal Reserve rate increases.

concept.explanation: Market capitalization, or market cap, is what the stock market says a whole company is worth: the share price multiplied by the number of shares. It moves whenever the share price moves, so when headlines say Nvidia "lost $573 billion" this week, no cash left the company; investors simply became willing to pay less for each share. Market cap matters to ordinary savers because the big index funds held in most 401(k) and retirement accounts weight companies by size. The larger a company's market cap, the bigger its slice of an S&P 500 fund, which is why a sharp fall in one giant company can dent the balance of someone who never bought its stock directly.
